check: Count red CI runs on dev over the next 10 merges to dev.
claim: Running CI on dev rather than main-only catches at least one failure on dev before it reaches main within the next 10 merges. If every dev run is green and main never regressed anyway, the extra CI is cost without signal.

check: py -3.11 -m pytest -q collects and passes; the new syntax-floor test enumerates every shipped script and reports how many failed ast.parse at feature_version=(3,9) before the fix.
claim: A mechanical 3.9-syntax guard plus a CI Python matrix will catch version-floor breakage that the OS matrix alone never could; I expect it to find at least one further 3.12-only construct beyond site.py:384 in the currently shipped scripts.

evidence: First half RIGHT: 3.11 went from cannot-collect to 785 passing, and the OS matrix could never have shown it (all three CI jobs pinned 3.12). Second half WRONG as stated: there was exactly ONE further 3.12-only construct, not more - the whole repo had a single one. But a second floor violation of a different kind did exist, 'import tomllib' at module scope (3.11 stdlib, not syntax), which the prediction did not anticipate because it assumed the problem was syntactic. The most useful outcome is that the CHECK I specified was invalid: ast.parse at feature_version=(3,9) reports the pre-fix file as CLEAN, because PEP 701 is a tokenizer change and feature_version only gates grammar. I had written down a measurement instrument that cannot measure the thing. The working guard needed three passes (tokenize, feature_version, AST import scan) plus a real-interpreter CI matrix.

check: Read the python-floor matrix results on the PR into dev: four jobs (3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.13). Record which interpreters failed and on what — a SyntaxError means python_floor.py missed something static and must be extended; a runtime TypeError/AttributeError means the static checker is working as designed and the gap is inherent to static checking.
claim: The new python-floor CI job will FAIL on Python 3.9 and/or 3.10 on its first run, because python_floor.py checks syntax and stdlib imports but cannot see runtime API usage (dict | merge, zip(strict=), 3.10-only kwargs). I grepped for the common ones and found none, but a grep is not an interpreter. I put this at roughly 40 percent. If it passes on all four, the 3.9+ promise is proven across its full declared range for the first time; if it fails, the gate caught on its first real outing exactly the class of defect it was built for, and the fix is a decision (patch the calls, or raise the floor to 3.11 and say so in the README) rather than a scramble.

evidence: 3.9 FAILED on first run; 3.10, 3.11 and 3.13 passed. Predicted '3.9 and/or 3.10' at ~40 percent - right, and right about which end of the range. But the MECHANISM was wrong in an instructive way. I predicted a runtime API failure in shipped code (dict | merge, zip(strict=)). Shipped code was fine: every other test collected and passed on 3.9, so the repo does honour its declared floor. What failed was my own test, asserting that --floor 3.10 ACCEPTS a match statement - which is false when the host is 3.9, because ast.parse feature_version can only make the parser stricter, never grant it grammar the host lacks. It is not a version simulator. That is the THIRD distinct way this one API misled me in a single session (the other two: PEP 701 is a tokenizer change so feature_version misses it entirely; and tomllib is not a syntax error at all). All three are now pinned by tests. Net: the matrix earned its place on its first run, catching a real defect that no local interpreter I had could show.
